title: Bara Masa, Tera Parba: osha, story and food
scope: Twelve selected profiles and a non-exhaustive expansion inventory. Five narrative checkpoints and seven early research notes; no complete statewide inventory or fully researched origin claim.

pages.name: Khudurukuni Osha
pages.lead: A small offering of rice carries a story of hunger, a sister’s hope and brothers away at sea.

sections.title: The story remembered
sections.text: In Deeti Ray’s account, Tapoi is the only sister of seven merchant brothers. During their absence, most of her sisters-in-law mistreat her. She encounters girls worshipping Mangala and offers the little khuda she has, asking for help. Her brothers return and discover her suffering. This is a ritual narrative, not a verified biography.
sections.locator: 2020 article, Tapoi narrative following the evening ritual

sections.title: Girls as keepers of the observance
sections.text: Ray describes Bhadraba Sundays in coastal Odisha: gathering flowers, a sand image called balunka, rice-paste decoration and evening recitation. Her photographs identify Pattamundai in Kendrapara as one setting. Girls organise and perform the worship. The account documents a particular cultural tradition; it does not establish identical practice in every district.

sections.title: Food makes the story tangible
sections.text: Patra’s 2019 essay identifies khuda as rice particles offered to Mangala. He connects the observance with a text attributed to Gopinath Das and with coastal maritime memory. The food association is stronger than any claim that a specific voyage occurred. Ray’s English food glosses sometimes use bran or husk; these are not interchangeable food-processing terms. We retain khuda and leave its preparation-specific identification for an Odia text and cook’s account.
sections.locator: Patra printed p.48; Ray food-offerings paragraph

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.text: An editorial reading of this story asks who receives care when a household’s earners are absent. The offering matters because of the giver’s circumstances. A food article can therefore follow rice through work, unequal access and devotion, rather than treating it only as a recipe. This interpretation should be tested against the words of present-day observers.

sections.title: History still to establish
sections.text: A twentieth- or twenty-first-century description is evidence that a tradition was recorded then, not its starting date. Manuscript and printed witnesses of the Tapoi text need to be compared before assigning a composition date. The 2022 journal paper has been located, but its original file was not recovered in this pass. Ray’s two publications would remain one author’s research lineage.

questions: How is khuda named and prepared in this locality?
Which Tapoi book or oral version is recited, and who taught it?
How have the worship group and food sharing changed?

pages.name: Manabasa Gurubara
pages.lead: A measure of grain becomes a way to think about sustenance, dignity and who may share a meal.

sections.title: Lakshmi and the rejected devotee
sections.text: Balabhadra Ghadai retells the Lakshmi Purana associated with Balaram Das: Lakshmi honours Sriya, a devotee identified in the narrative as Chandala. Balabhadra objects to the visit, and Jagannath excludes Lakshmi. The conflict centres on caste and the goddess’s freedom to recognise devotion. This is the text’s story, not evidence that discrimination subsequently disappeared.
sections.locator: Cult of Goddess Mahalakshmi, printed p.102

sections.title: Hunger changes the argument
sections.text: The Mohantys’ 2021 essay describes the brothers’ hardship after Lakshmi leaves and reads the work as a challenge to caste barriers. Food becomes central to the dispute over authority. Our interpretation is that a household’s feeding labour is made visible through its withdrawal: those who dismiss its source discover their dependence on it.

sections.title: The meal and the recognition
sections.text: In Ghadai’s retelling, the hungry brothers reach Lakshmi’s new household. Told that its mistress is Chandala, they first attempt to cook for themselves and fail. They finally accept her cooked food, recognise its familiar preparation and reunite with her. The reversal makes exclusion answerable to the experience of hunger. Ghadai himself says the story’s time of formation is not definitely known.

sections.title: The household observance
sections.text: The same essay places the worship on Margasira Thursdays and identifies the mana or grain measure among its objects. Dash records khiri, khechudi, kakara and chakuli as associated foods. These are attributed examples, not a compulsory menu for every Thursday or home.

sections.title: A history of text, voice and work
sections.text: The next historical step is to identify dated editions and manuscripts of Lakshmi Purana and compare how they are read aloud. The author attribution alone does not date today’s menu or decorations. The collection should credit the reader, cook and person who draws the household designs, including work that a dish photograph would leave invisible.

sections.title: A visitor’s starting point
sections.text: Learn the meaning of the grain measure and ask a willing cook about one preparation. A shop selling chakuli does not provide access to a household’s Manabasa worship. A future tasting record needs its own date, provider and consent.

questions: Which edition or inherited oral passage is used?
Which offerings differ across the Thursdays?
What does the family say about Sriya and shared food?

pages.name: Sudasa Brata
pages.lead: A knotted thread and an offering of manda connect a recurring vow with Lakshmi.

sections.title: The vow and its objects
sections.text: The Mohantys describe a thread with ten knots, each associated with a name of Lakshmi. Mahanti gives the calendrical condition as a Thursday coinciding with the bright fortnight’s tenth lunar day; it can recur within a year. Dash’s Kartika-only description is therefore retained as a conflict, not used as the general rule.
sections.locator: Mohanty p.25; Mahanti p.43; Dash p.15

sections.title: Manda in the offering
sections.text: Dash names manda for Sudasa. The existing food record describes a steamed version, but that does not establish the recipe of every ritual offering. The useful questions concern dough, filling, cooking method, number and distribution. A dish name can remain stable while its preparation varies.

sections.title: What history can and cannot say
sections.text: The sources connect the brata to Lakshmi devotion; they do not establish an earliest Odisha performance in this study. Mahanti’s claim of revival by Balarama Das needs a dated textual witness before becoming our chronology. The knot’s significance should be narrated from an identified katha, rather than completed from an unrelated internet version.

sections.title: Reading its significance
sections.text: A useful editorial lens is the relationship between an enduring object and repeated action: a thread can remind its wearer of a vow between observances. This is a question to explore with practitioners, not an assertion that everyone gives the thread the same meaning.

questions: Which Sudasa katha and edition supplies the local story?
How are the old thread and new thread treated?
Is the local manda steamed or fried, and what is its filling?

pages.name: Dutiya Osha
pages.lead: The path from offered produce to a shared ghanta is the beginning of this food story.

sections.title: A documented sequence
sections.text: Dash’s 2006 essay records fruits and vegetables offered during Dutiya Osha and cooked into ghanta the following day. He also mentions sand figures of a fox and a bird. The source groups several names together; we have not treated that as proof that every regional Jitiya or Puajiuntia tradition is identical.

sections.title: Food after the offering
sections.text: The important research unit is the sequence: gathering, offering, cooking and sharing. A recipe alone would miss the change in the produce’s ritual role. The next account should identify a particular household’s ghanta, its ingredients and recipients; it should also record omissions and substitutions. This is an editorial approach, not a measured claim about waste reduction or nutrition.

sections.title: The missing narrative
sections.text: The fox-and-bird figures point to a story that needs an identified local katha. This page deliberately does not import a neighbouring region’s narrative to fill the gap. No foundation date or earliest local manuscript has yet been established.

sections.title: For the seasonal guide
sections.text: Ghanta can be explored as a dish beyond this observance. A visitor listing must say whether a provider offers an everyday version or an observance-associated preparation, and on which confirmed dates.

questions: What are the local name and bird identification in the katha?
Which produce is offered, and which is cooked the following day?
Who receives a share, and how is the dish named?

pages.name: Budhei Osha
pages.lead: Kitchen grinding stones open a line of inquiry into household worship and hopes for children.

sections.title: The record we have
sections.text: Dash places Budhei on Bhadraba Wednesdays and describes worship involving a grinding stone. Mahanti records fruit and pitha offerings, with a coconut kept from the first Wednesday to the last. Their deity identifications differ. We preserve those accounts rather than selecting one identity as definitive.

sections.title: Everyday objects, sacred roles
sections.text: The grinding stone makes this a promising study of the relationship between food labour and household ritual. That is our research lens; the object alone cannot prove the observance began in a particular occupation, century or religious school. Its handling, decoration and return to everyday use need an attributed local account.

sections.title: Story and food gaps
sections.text: A full narrative needs a named Budhei or Budhibaman text and a comparison of its episodes. Neither a universal pitha menu nor a uniform fasting practice is established here. We should ask who selects the foods and how the final Wednesday differs, while leaving fertility and protection claims explicitly within belief.

questions: Are Budhei, Sudhei and Budhibaman distinguished locally?
Which stories are read on successive Wednesdays?
What foods belong to the final observance?

pages.name: Alana Osha
pages.lead: A food restriction can be as culturally meaningful as a festive dish.

sections.title: Agreement and disagreement
sections.text: Dash describes Alana as an Ashwina observance without salt and associates it with Lakshmi. Mahanti also describes unsalted offerings but names Surya. This is an unresolved source difference; neither a single deity nor a uniform household practice is asserted.

sections.title: Narrating restraint
sections.text: The next page should ask what observers mean by the restriction, what they actually prepare and when they resume ordinary food. It would be misleading to attach a generic sweet to Alana simply to fill a menu. A cultural description of abstention is not dietary advice or evidence of a health benefit.

sections.title: History to recover
sections.text: No securely dated origin or inspected local ritual narrative has been established. The conflict may involve regional variation, terminology or an error; that question needs evidence, not a harmonised story invented by the editor.

questions: Which deity and katha does the household recognise?
Does the restriction apply to offerings, the observer’s meals or both?

pages.name: Kanji Anla Osha
pages.lead: Rice-water preparations and a ritual offering invite a closer look at a less-documented part of the food year.

sections.title: What the sources describe
sections.text: Dash associates Kanji Anla with Sathi and lists kanji, radish and other materials. Mahanti describes kanji from fermented rice gruel and dried-fish offerings in an evening observance. The accounts should be compared locally; the study does not turn their lists into one standard recipe.

sections.title: A food-science question
sections.text: There is a worthwhile distinction between recording a fermentation practice and measuring it. A future preparation record should identify ingredients, water, vessel, temperature, time and subsequent cooking. These variables are research questions; we have not tested this preparation, identified its organisms or demonstrated a probiotic benefit.

sections.title: The narrative remains open
sections.text: A local katha, historical editions and the relationship to Sathi or Sasthi need further study. The use of dried fish also means that a blanket claim that all osha offerings are vegetarian would erase relevant evidence. This page retains the difference without claiming every household follows it.

food_names: dried fish in an attributed account
questions: Which kanji preparation and local name are used?
How do observers explain the offered materials?
How does the practice relate to Prathamastami in this locality?

pages.name: Bada Osha
pages.lead: A Shiva offering called gaja needs its own identity, separate from sweets sold under similar names.

sections.title: Food with a ritual form
sections.text: The Jagatsinghpur district gazetteer describes a steamed gaja offering shaped as a linga and snake, followed by the breaking of a fast. This is a district account, not a verified menu at every Shiva temple. The preparation must not be silently equated with the fried chhena gaja in an existing food catalogue.

sections.title: Why location matters
sections.text: Mahanti associates Bada Osha particularly with Dhabaleswar and gives Kartika’s bright thirteenth or fourteenth day. The Jagatsinghpur gazetteer mentions Kartika Purnima. We keep those calendar statements separate pending a temple-specific annual schedule and clarification of observance versus culmination.

sections.title: History and significance
sections.text: The evidence supports a connection among fasting, offering and Shiva worship. An origin story needs a traceable text or temple account before being narrated as the local explanation. Even then, the legend and the dated history of the shrine will remain separate.

sections.title: A visitor’s next step
sections.text: A future guide can explain what the offering means, but temple access, crowd arrangements and distribution need current checks. No ticket, serving time or availability is established by this historical description.

questions: What does the Dhabaleswar authority call the offering and its preparation?
Which date marks the fast and which marks its breaking?

pages.name: Samba Dashami
pages.lead: An offering made in a child’s name makes a family’s hopes visible through food.

sections.title: The legend and the observance
sections.text: Dina Krishna Joshi’s 2013 essay recounts the belief that Samba, Krishna’s son, recovered from illness through devotion to Surya. It places the observance on Pausa’s bright tenth lunar day. The healing belongs to sacred narrative; it is neither clinical evidence nor a dated account of the festival’s beginnings.

sections.title: A family written in food
sections.text: Joshi describes offerings associated with individual family members and foods including khichdi, ghadghadia tarkari, pitha and khiri. His account moves through morning, midday and evening acts of worship and subsequent sharing. This gives us a sequence to investigate, not a universal menu or timetable.

sections.title: Sun worship in the landscape
sections.text: A multidisciplinary 2015 study of Konark records Samba Dashami among traditions associated with Chandrabhaga. That association is distinct from the study’s investigation of a lost river. A ritual’s relationship to a place does not date the ritual or establish the location of every episode in its legend.
sections.locator: Printed p.94, Rituals and Festivals associated with the river

sections.title: What gives the food its meaning
sections.text: Our interpretive question is how an offering in someone’s name becomes a household memory. Which item belongs to which child? Does it remain the same after that person leaves home? Those questions could connect the historical reading with living family accounts, without claiming interviews have already taken place.

questions: When and why was a particular offering chosen?
Which foods and worship times differ locally?
Which Samba katha is recited?

pages.name: Prathamastami
pages.lead: Enduri’s leaf wrapping connects a food technique with an occasion centred on the eldest child.

sections.title: Family and food
sections.text: Mahanti describes honouring the eldest child, including new clothes and an offering of enduri. Odisha Tourism independently associates enduri with Prathamastami and describes turmeric-leaf wrapping with a coconut-jaggery filling. These support a cultural food connection, not a claim that enduri is unavailable at other times.
sections.locator: Mahanti p.59; Tourism Enduri Pitha section

sections.title: What the leaf contributes
sections.text: The existing enduri page is the preparation reference. The observance page asks a different question: how does making, offering and sharing that food express a family relationship? We should record the leaf, batter, filling, steamer and cook alongside the person being honoured, rather than allow the recipe to replace the occasion.

sections.title: The calendar and history
sections.text: Margasira is supported in the household account, but earlier indexed temple descriptions differed on the fortnight. The website therefore does not generate a current date. A dated panji and a locality-specific check are needed. The earliest evidence of the household practice is also still to be established.

questions: What role do maternal relatives play in this family’s celebration?
Which enduri version is used and who makes it?
What dated calendar governs the local observance?

pages.name: Sabitri Brata
pages.lead: Savitri’s conversation with Yama gives this observance a literary history that can be read directly.

sections.title: A woman follows and argues
sections.text: In the Mahabharata passage preserved in K. M. Ganguli’s translation, Satyavan collapses while collecting wood. When Yama takes his life, Savitri follows. She speaks about duty, friendship and compassion; Yama repeatedly grants boons while withholding Satyavan’s life. Her request for children through Satyavan exposes the contradiction. He is restored. The episode gives Savitri a sustained speaking and reasoning role, not merely a moment of passive waiting.
sections.locator: Vana Parva, section displayed as CCLXLV, printed pp.576–581

sections.title: Textual history is not a local origin date
sections.text: An epic passage is direct evidence for the story. It does not tell us when a particular Odisha household began its annual brata or when its food customs took shape. That requires Odia katha editions, local histories and carefully attributed practice accounts. The pan-Indian story and the regional observance are connected research subjects, not interchangeable records.
sections.locator: Scope of the inspected epic passage

sections.title: Seasonal offerings
sections.text: Mahanti records a Jyestha new-moon observance with fruit offerings. Exact fruit selections need a local account; no fixed shopping list is prescribed here. Food can be documented through its role as an offering and its sharing after the observance, with changes in seasonal availability left visible.

sections.title: Significance to explore
sections.text: The literary conversation permits questions about resolve, love and moral reasoning. Present-day observers may emphasise different aspects. A responsible narrative should let those explanations coexist and avoid turning a description of married women’s practice into a duty imposed on readers.

questions: Which Odia Savitri katha is read?
Which fruits are chosen locally, and how are they shared?
What aspects of Savitri’s words matter most to the observer?

pages.name: Janhi Osha
pages.lead: A vegetable plant enters the ritual year through its flowers, not just through the kitchen.

sections.title: The surviving outline
sections.text: Dash associates Janhi with Tulsi worship and its culmination at Kumar Purnima. Mahanti describes girls arranging ridge-gourd flowers to reflect the moon’s changing appearance. He explicitly leaves its origin unknown. The descriptions provide a starting point for documentation, not a dated beginning or proof of a statewide pattern.

sections.title: A food-culture question without an invented menu
sections.text: Janhi is a food plant, but that does not establish ridge-gourd curry as the observance’s special dish. Its flowers have a ritual role in the inspected account. The study should document that role first and ask separately about offerings and meals. Keeping these distinctions protects a small tradition from being rewritten as a generic food festival.

sections.title: What to recover next
sections.text: Local songs, a dated account and present-day explanations of the floral designs are the next evidence. The relationship between Janhi Osha and Kumar Purnima should be described without collapsing them into one event. No named food offering or current participation arrangement is established here.

questions: Which flowers and patterns are used on successive evenings?
Which song explains the observance locally?
What food, if any, belongs specifically to Janhi rather than Kumar Purnima?
